notes.meaning: The residents of Kiriath-jearim gladly took the ark of God into Abinadab's home on a hill. They appointed his son Eleazar to guard and care for it with reverence. Even though the ark was placed in a private home rather than a public tent of worship, God provided a safe and honored resting place for it.

The ark stayed at Kiriath-jearim for a long period, and twenty years passed before the people finally woke up to their spiritual need. During these quiet years, the people of Israel mourned their distance from God and began longing for His presence once more. Genuine spiritual renewal often starts with a deep sorrow over leaving the Lord.

Samuel told the people that crying out was not enough; they had to prove their repentance by turning back to God with all their hearts. He urged them to get rid of their pagan idols and false goddesses, promise total loyalty to the Lord, and serve Him alone. Samuel assured them that if their hearts were right, God would rescue them from Philistine control.

The people listened to Samuel's call and threw out the images of the local gods, Baal and Ashtoreth. They chose to put away their favorite false worship and serve the Lord alone. Outward actions showed that their inward sorrow was real.

Samuel called the whole nation to gather at the hilltop town of Mizpah for a sacred assembly. He promised to stand before God as their intercessor and pray on their behalf. True leaders seek God in prayer for the people they lead.

At Mizpah, the people poured out water on the ground to show their brokenness and deep sorrow over their sins. They went without food for the day and openly confessed that they had sinned against the Lord. Samuel also began to lead the nation there by teaching God's ways and settling disputes.

When the Philistine rulers heard that Israel had gathered at Mizpah, they suspected a rebellion and marched up with an army. The Israelites had come together to pray rather than fight, so learning about the advancing army made them terrified. Turning to God does not mean we will never face scary moments.

Instead of trusting in military weapons or trying to carry the ark into battle as a good-luck charm, the people begged Samuel to keep praying. They asked him not to stop crying out to the Lord so that God would rescue them from the Philistines. They had learned that their only real safety was in God's help.

Samuel offered a young nursing lamb as a whole burnt offering, showing the complete dedication of the people to God. As the smoke rose, he cried out to the Lord on Israel's behalf, and the Lord heard and answered his prayer. God honors sincere prayer when it is paired with wholehearted devotion.

Just as the Philistines moved in to attack, the Lord sent a massive roar of thunder that threw the enemy into a wild panic. The Philistines lost their courage, broke ranks, and fled in terror before Israel. God proved that He had full power over the storm and could protect His people without their weapons.

The men of Israel rushed down from Mizpah and chased the fleeing Philistines across the countryside. They struck down the enemy soldiers until they reached the area beneath Beth-car. God gave them the courage to finish the victory that He had begun.

After the battle, Samuel set up a large standing stone between Mizpah and Shen to remember what God had done. He named it Ebenezer, which means 'Stone of Help,' declaring that the Lord had helped them all the way up to that moment. Looking back at God's past help gives His people hope for the future.

The Philistines were brought low by this crushing defeat and stopped launching major invasions into Israelite territory. The Lord continued to stand against them and keep Israel safe throughout Samuel's lifetime as judge. When a nation walks in obedience, God shields them from their oppressors.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view the statement that the Philistines invaded no more as part of an independent tradition, since later chapters record ongoing Philistine battles during Saul's reign.

notes.meaning: The towns along the border between Ekron and Gath that had been captured by the Philistines were returned to Israel. Israel also freed the surrounding lands from enemy control, and the neighboring Amorite tribes kept peace with them as well. When God's people live in His favor, even longtime enemies often cease their attacks.

Samuel served as the judge and spiritual guide of Israel for his entire life. Even after Saul was chosen as king, Samuel continued to offer counsel, teach God's laws, and carry moral authority over the nation. Faithful service to God lasts throughout a believer's whole life.

Each year Samuel traveled a regular circuit between the historic towns of Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah. In each town he heard complaints, solved disputes, and taught the people how to obey God's laws. He took the trouble to travel so that ordinary people could easily reach justice.

After finishing his circuit, Samuel always went back home to Ramah, where he lived and held court for the people. He also built an altar to the Lord there so he and the community could offer sacrifices and worship. Because the tabernacle at Shiloh was gone, Samuel used his authority as a prophet to keep true worship alive.
